_note: The Sentence Lock dials: for every sentence in the shared sentence bank, one dial per Tongan word with its role label, the book's word (right) and the options in a fixed order (the right word plus up to three wrong ones of the same kind). `sources` names where each option comes from, parallel to `options`. Built by build-dials.mjs from sentence-bank.json and book-vocabulary.json under the rules below; every Tongan string comes from those two files. Do not edit by hand; rebuild.

rules.what: Same kind: a wrong option has the same role label as the right word. Sources in order: the bank's words with that role; for tense marker and pronoun the bank's tenseTable and pronounTable; for possessive the book's possessive tables (Lesson 17 lines 37 to 80, possessives.json); for verb, noun, adjective, modifier, time word and name also the matching entries of book-vocabulary.json. Words of the sentence's own lesson and earlier lessons come first; later lessons fill only when earlier ones run short.

No other tense marker of the same tense as the right one, and no two options of one tense, so the past markers never sit together on one dial. Where the English says "is/are/am" with a state and no "-ing" word ("is tired"), the present and perfect markers count as one tense, because the book glosses both as the state. Where the English is "is/are/am" + "-ing" with no future cue (no will, tomorrow, soon, going to ...), no future marker is offered, because the book renders such English with a future marker in places.

A pronoun option never has the same person as the subject the English names, unless the English itself marks the number or inclusiveness that rules it out ("(one person)", "(exclusive, three or more)", "(not including you)", "(two)", "(to a group)"). "You" without such a mark excludes every other second-person pronoun. The general "one" pronoun (the table row glossed "one") is never a wrong option where the English subject is "I" or "you", marked or not, because the book uses it for English "you" and "I" in general statements.

Another form of the same pronoun (the I forms) is a wrong option only where the pronoun table's book lines settle that it does not follow the right tense marker: the right word's line says which markers it follows ("after ...") and the option's line does not name that marker.

No option clashes with the right word under fair.js clashes() (shared content word, shared meaning item, same spelling, derived pair, confusable pair), and no two wrong options clash with each other. Pairs the book uses for the same English meaning, kept in equivalents.json beside the builder (the shared confusable-pairs.json is untouched), clash too.
No option equals the right word or another option after okinafy display and case-folding; an accent-only variant of the same word counts as equal.
No option whose meaning shares a content word with the sentence's English prompt (it could be the book's own word for that English word).

Every word on a dial except tense markers, pronouns and names has a meaning in the course vocabulary, so R2d and R2f could be run on it; a word without one is fixed, and a candidate without one is not offered. The lookup ignores acute accents and macrons, so a word and its vocabulary spelling match. A preposition the vocabulary gives no meaning (the one glossed "with") is still live: its options are checked against the English by R2f, small words such as "with" and "from" included, and against each other by R2d. A possessive is checked against the book's possessive tables instead (R2j).

Where the English says "a", "an" or "some" and the noun carries no final-vowel accent, the two articles the vocabulary glosses "a, some" and "the" (equivalents.json) are not wrong options for each other, because the book writes the English "a basket" with either. The article used only before one word class stays fair where its position rules it out.

A direction word (the directional particle role) is a dial only where the English marks the direction (come, toward, around, up, down, away, here). Where the English only names the action ("return"), no direction word is a sure wrong answer, so the word is fixed.

A possessive is a dial when the book's possessive tables (Lesson 17) have a row for it. Its options are rows of the same class (e-class or ho-class) with another person than the right word, whatever the number, and no option whose table gloss shares a content word with the English.

No give-away by spelling. A tense marker option shows the form the book prints in that position (the bank's accented form before a one-syllable pronoun, the bare form otherwise). For every other word the option shows a form with the same accent state as the right word, taken from the bank or the vocabulary; a word with no such form is not offered. Trailing punctuation of the right word is copied onto the options. A pronoun that follows a word whose stress accent depends on the pronoun (the tense markers, and any word the bank prints accented before a one-syllable pronoun) is offered only with pronouns of the right word's number of vowels, so the accent on the word to its left never narrows the dial to one answer.

Every option string comes from sentence-bank.json, book-vocabulary.json or the book's Lesson 17 possessive tables in possessives.json (apart from the trailing punctuation copied from the right word). Words in LEFT_OUT_OF_GAME never appear.
A word whose role is null is fixed (shown in place, no dial; why "no label in the book"). A word with no fair wrong option is fixed too, with its reason.
